# Risk rules

<!-- Generated by `pnpm docs:rules` from the rule metadata in `packages/core/src/rules/`. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every finding carries its rule id, a severity, concrete evidence and where the information comes from (provenance).
The verdict is `critical` if any critical finding; otherwise `incomplete` if the analysis has any gap; otherwise `attention` if any warning; otherwise `no-findings` (shown as “No findings from the checks performed”, never as “safe”).
Findings about an instruction inside a Squads proposal that the analysed transaction only creates are marked as proposed: they happen only if that proposal is later approved and executed.

## Critical

### VGL-C001 — Program upgrade

**What it checks.** A BPF Upgradeable Loader `Upgrade` instruction: the program's code is replaced with the contents of a buffer account.

**Why it matters.** After the upgrade the program can do anything its new code allows, including moving every asset it controls. What matters is exactly which code is in the buffer, so the finding shows the buffer, its executable hash and the program's current verification status.

**False positives.** Every legitimate upgrade fires this rule too: it is critical because an upgrade replaces all of a program's behaviour, not because upgrades are suspicious. Compare the buffer's executable hash with the verified build you expect.

### VGL-C002 — Upgrade authority change

**What it checks.** A BPF Upgradeable Loader `SetAuthority` or `SetAuthorityChecked` on a program's ProgramData account or on a buffer.

**Why it matters.** Whoever holds a program's upgrade authority can replace its code at any time. Giving it to an address outside this multisig hands over full control of the program; removing it makes the program immutable forever.

**False positives.** Handing the upgrade authority to this multisig's own vault (for example when moving a program under multisig control) still fires, with the milder wording. Making a program immutable on purpose also fires: it is irreversible, so it is always worth a second look.

### VGL-C003 — Token authority change

**What it checks.** Any SPL Token or Token-2022 `SetAuthority` (mint, freeze, account owner, close and every extension authority), and the Token-2022 metadata and group update-authority changes.

**Why it matters.** Token authorities decide who can mint new tokens, freeze accounts, move or close accounts, or change a token's fees, hooks and metadata. Handing one over gives that power to someone else without another vote.

**False positives.** Routine hand-overs (for example moving a mint authority to a new multisig) fire too. Removing an authority for good (for example fixing a token's supply) also fires, because it is irreversible.

### VGL-C004 — Delegate approval

**What it checks.** An SPL Token or Token-2022 `Approve` or `ApproveChecked`.

**Why it matters.** A delegate can move up to the approved amount out of the token account at any time, without another vote of the multisig.

**False positives.** Some protocols legitimately ask for a delegate (for example an escrow or a lending position). The finding shows the delegate and the amount so it can be checked against what was intended.

### VGL-C005 — Account owner change

**What it checks.** A System Program `Assign` or `AssignWithSeed`.

**Why it matters.** The owner program has full control over an account's data and lamports. Assigning a vault or any funded account to another program hands its contents to that program.

**False positives.** Creating a new account for a program (`CreateAccount`) does not fire. `Assign` on a freshly allocated account is part of some legitimate set-up flows; check that the account is new and holds nothing.

### VGL-C006 — Multisig configuration change

**What it checks.** A change to this multisig's settings: add or remove a member, change the threshold (stronger if lowered), change the time lock (stronger if lowered), set the rent collector, add or remove a spending limit, or change the config authority. Found in a config proposal, in a proposal being created in the analysed transaction, or in a direct config-authority instruction.

**Why it matters.** These change who can approve and execute transactions and how fast. A spending limit lets its members spend up to its amount without any vote. Attackers who get one proposal through often use it to lower the threshold or add their own member.

**False positives.** Every settings change fires, including routine ones such as adding a new member or raising the threshold: they all change who controls the vaults. Lowering the threshold or the time lock gets the stronger wording.

### VGL-C007 — Stake authority change

**What it checks.** A Stake Program `Authorize`, `AuthorizeChecked`, `AuthorizeWithSeed`, `AuthorizeCheckedWithSeed`, or a `SetLockup` / `SetLockupChecked` that sets a new lockup custodian. Vote-account authority changes cannot be detected: the Vote program is not decoded (they show as an opaque instruction, VGL-W001).

**Why it matters.** The withdraw authority can take all the stake; the staker can redirect it; the custodian can lift a lockup. Changing any of them hands that power to the new address.

**False positives.** Moving stake accounts to a new custody set-up fires too. `SetLockup` that only changes the lockup dates (no new custodian) does not fire.

### VGL-C008 — Possible address poisoning

**What it checks.** An address in the transaction that is not known, but shares its first four and last four characters with a known address: a member, a vault, the multisig, a registry program or token, one of your known addresses, or a recent destination.

**Why it matters.** Address poisoning: attackers generate look-alike addresses so that a signer who only checks the start and end of an address approves sending funds, or authority, to the attacker.

**False positives.** Two unrelated addresses sharing the same first and last four characters by chance is very unlikely (about one in 58⁸), so a match is almost always deliberate. Add the address to your known addresses if it really is yours. Addresses ending in twelve or more `1`s (native program and sysvar ids, which are constructed rather than generated and cannot be ground by an attacker) are never reported.

### VGL-C009 — Account closed to an external destination

**What it checks.** An SPL Token / Token-2022 `CloseAccount`, or a BPF Upgradeable Loader `Close`, whose lamports go to an address that is not a vault of this multisig (or one of your known addresses).

**Why it matters.** Closing sends everything the account holds in lamports to the recipient; closing a program's ProgramData account also deletes the program for good.

**False positives.** Closing an empty token account and sending its rent to a member's own wallet fires too (a member is not a vault). In base64 mode, with no multisig to compare with, any recipient that is not a signer of the transaction or one of your known addresses counts as external.

### VGL-C010 — Unresolvable message

**What it checks.** The transaction cannot be fully resolved: a lookup table is missing or invalid, an account index points outside the transaction, a transaction carried inside a Squads instruction cannot be decoded, or a Squads instruction itself is malformed.

**Why it matters.** If the accounts an instruction touches cannot be established, nobody can say what it will do. A proposal built so that it cannot be displayed is a known way to hide its effect.

**False positives.** A lookup table that was closed after the proposal was created makes an old proposal unresolvable too; it then also cannot be executed as it stands.

### VGL-C011 — Upgrade buffer with external authority

**What it checks.** A loader `Upgrade` whose buffer's authority (read from chain) is not the upgrade authority signing the upgrade (this multisig's vault).

**Why it matters.** Whoever controls the buffer can rewrite its contents after the vote and hand the buffer to the vault just before execution: members would approve one program and deploy another.

**False positives.** None expected: for the upgrade to succeed the buffer authority must equal the program's upgrade authority, so a buffer controlled by someone else is either a mistake or an opportunity to swap its contents before execution.

## Warning

### VGL-W001 — Opaque instruction

**What it checks.** An instruction Vigil cannot decode: the program has no built-in decoder and no readable IDL, or its data does not match what the decoder expects.

**Why it matters.** Nobody can say what an opaque instruction does from the transaction alone: it may move funds, change authorities, or do nothing at all.

**False positives.** Programs that publish no IDL fire even when they are well known. Adding a decoder or publishing an IDL (Program Metadata) removes the warning.

### VGL-W002 — Program not verified

**What it checks.** A program the transaction calls whose deployed code is not a verified build of public source code, or whose verification status could not be established.

**Why it matters.** Without a verified build, nobody can check that the deployed code matches any published source.

**False positives.** Many honest programs are not verified builds. Programs in Vigil's curated registry (native programs, SPL Token, Squads) are not checked. When the verification service cannot be reached the status is unknown and the analysis is also marked incomplete.

### VGL-W003 — Program upgradeable by a third party

**What it checks.** A program the transaction calls that can be upgraded by an authority other than this multisig's vaults (or your known addresses).

**Why it matters.** Its code can be replaced after members vote and before the proposal executes, so what the program does at execution time may differ from what was reviewed.

**False positives.** Most actively maintained protocols are upgradeable by their own team or multisig; that is expected, but it means their behaviour can change between the vote and execution. Programs in the curated registry are not checked.

### VGL-W004 — Large transfer

**What it checks.** SOL or token transfers that together move at least `largeTransferPercent` of the sending account's balance in that asset, or at least the absolute amount configured for that asset.

**Why it matters.** Draining a vault is the most common goal of a malicious proposal. Seeing the share of the balance at stake helps catch a proposal that moves far more than expected.

**False positives.** Planned large payments (treasury moves, payroll) fire too; the threshold (`largeTransferPercent`, default 10 % of the sending account's balance in that asset, and optional per-asset absolute amounts) can be tuned. Several transfers of the same asset from the same account are added up, so splitting a payment does not hide it. When the balance could not be read and no absolute threshold is set, the transfer cannot be judged and the analysis is marked incomplete instead.

### VGL-W005 — New destination

**What it checks.** A transfer to an address that received nothing in the vault's last `historyDepth` transactions.

**Why it matters.** Attackers substitute their own address for a familiar one. A destination the vault has never paid before deserves a careful check of the full address.

**False positives.** Paying someone for the first time fires. Only runs when `historyDepth` is above 0; this multisig's vaults and your known addresses are never reported.

### VGL-W006 — Simulation failed or unavailable

**What it checks.** Simulation was attempted and either failed or could not be run.

**Why it matters.** Simulation is the only independent view of the balances a transaction will actually change. Without it the balance checks (VGL-W007) cannot run.

**False positives.** A proposal whose time lock has not passed, or that depends on state that will only exist later, can fail to simulate today and still execute correctly. If you turned simulation off this rule does not fire; the analysis is marked incomplete instead.

### VGL-W007 — Unexpected balance changes

**What it checks.** The simulation changes the balance of an account that no decoded instruction lists as writable.

**Why it matters.** A balance change nothing in the decoded transaction explains means something is happening that the summary does not show.

**False positives.** Programs that move funds through accounts they do not list as writable in the decoded instruction (for example through a CPI into an opaque program) fire. The fee payer's own SOL decrease (the transaction fee) is not reported.

### VGL-W008 — Impersonating token

**What it checks.** A token whose declared symbol or name looks like a registry token's (after Unicode normalization, mapping look-alike characters and ignoring case and punctuation) but whose mint differs; or whose declared name or symbol contains invisible, control, bidirectional or non-ASCII characters, or mixes scripts.

**Why it matters.** Anyone can create a token called “USDC”. Fake tokens that look like real ones are used to disguise what a transfer really moves.

**False positives.** Wrapped or bridged versions of a registry token (for example another issuer's USDC) fire, because their declared name matches but the mint is not the registry one. Tokens with non-Latin names fire the suspicious-characters variant. Only registry tokens of the same cluster are compared.

### VGL-W009 — Durable nonce

**What it checks.** In base64 mode: the transaction starts with a System `AdvanceNonceAccount`, so it uses a durable nonce instead of a recent blockhash (the runtime only treats instruction 0 this way).

**Why it matters.** A durable-nonce transaction never expires: once signed, it can be submitted at any later time by whoever holds it, long after the signer has forgotten about it.

**False positives.** Offline and hardware-wallet signing flows use durable nonces legitimately.

### VGL-W010 — Fragile multisig

**What it checks.** The multisig's threshold is 1 (any single member can approve alone), or it has a config authority that can change its settings without a vote.

**Why it matters.** One compromised key is then enough to take control: through a single approval, or through the config authority.

**False positives.** Some teams deliberately run a 1-of-N multisig, or keep a config authority for recovery. The warning describes the multisig itself, not this proposal.

### VGL-W011 — Incomplete analysis

**What it checks.** The analysis has at least one gap: something could not be read, decoded, simulated or verified.

**Why it matters.** The absence of findings means nothing about the parts that could not be analysed.

**False positives.** None: any gap means part of the transaction could not be checked. It is always shown first so an empty findings list is never mistaken for a clean result.

## Info

### VGL-I001 — Compute budget and priority fee

**What it checks.** The compute budget the transaction requests: compute-unit limit and price, and the maximum priority fee that results (Compute Budget instructions, or a v1 transaction's inline settings). Compute Budget instructions inside a Squads proposal are also listed, with a note that they have no effect there.

**Why it matters.** The priority fee is paid by the fee payer on top of the base fee. Inside a proposal, Compute Budget instructions do nothing (the program is a no-op when invoked; the runtime only reads them at the top level of a transaction).

**False positives.** Informational.

### VGL-I002 — Memo

**What it checks.** A Memo program instruction, with its text (sanitized: control, bidirectional and invisible characters removed).

**Why it matters.** Memos are free text written by whoever built the transaction. They can describe the transaction honestly, or be written to mislead; they do not change what it does.

**False positives.** Informational.

### VGL-I003 — Address lookup tables used

**What it checks.** Address lookup tables the transaction (or the proposal) loads accounts from.

**Why it matters.** Accounts loaded from a table are not written in the transaction itself. Existing table entries can never change (tables are append-only), so what was resolved now is what will be used, as long as the table is not closed.

**False positives.** Informational.

### VGL-I004 — Proposal status

**What it checks.** The proposal's status: approvals against the threshold, rejections, cancellations, the time lock, and how long until it can be executed.

**Why it matters.** Knowing how many approvals are still needed, and when the proposal becomes executable, tells members how much time is left to review it.

**False positives.** Informational.

### VGL-I005 — Stale proposal

**What it checks.** The proposal can no longer be executed: it was rejected, cancelled or already executed; or it is stale (a settings change happened after it was created) and either is a config proposal, or was not approved before becoming stale.

**Why it matters.** Voting on it has no effect. Staleness rules are those of the Squads v4 program: stale config transactions can never execute; stale vault and batch transactions can only if already approved.

**False positives.** None: the proposal cannot be executed. Note that a stale vault or batch proposal that was approved before becoming stale can still be executed, so it does not fire.
